issues.legal_issue: A statute enacted within legislative competence cannot be invalidated solely for vagueness, and an undefined term may be applied according to its ordinary meaning.
material_facts: The original legislation regulated and reserved the holding of cattle fairs to the State but did not define “cattle fair”.

The legislation concerned fairs, an area within the State Legislature’s competence, and the expression had an ordinary meaning as a periodic gathering of buyers and sellers, generally for the sale and purchase of cattle, at times or occasions ordained by custom.
The earlier challenge treated vagueness, rather than violation of an express constitutional limitation, as the basis for invalidating the statute.
issues.conclusion: The original legislation was not unenforceable for vagueness because the undefined expression could be given its ordinary meaning; in any event, vagueness alone was not a ground on which a court could invalidate it.
issues.legal_principle: A court may invalidate legislation where the legislature lacked competence, the law violates a fundamental right, or it conflicts with another constitutional provision, but not merely because it is vague. The doctrine of due process has no place in the constitutional system, as held in A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, [1950] SCR 88. An undefined statutory expression may be understood in its ordinary signification.

predicates.legislation_within_legislative_competenc: The legislature enacted the statute on a subject within its lawmaking competence.
predicates.challenge_based_only_on_vagueness: The challenger relied on uncertainty in the statute, rather than establishing that it violated an express constitutional limitation.

issues.definition: If a competent legislature enacts a statute and the challenge relies only on vagueness, the statute is not invalidated on that ground alone.

issues.legal_issue: A prior judgment invalidating legislation for vagueness does not create res judicata preventing enforcement after the asserted defect is remedied by amendment.
material_facts: An earlier judgment had treated the original legislation as invalid because it did not define “cattle fair”.
The legislature later amended the statute to define a cattle fair as a gathering of more than twenty-five persons for the purpose of general sale or purchase of cattle.
The later challenge was brought after that amendment.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgment did not operate as res judicata against enforcement of the amended legislation; the amendment remedied the defect identified in that judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The earlier judgment did not render the statute permanently nonexistent or bar a later challenge after the legislature amended it. Its stated effect was confined to the statute as it stood without a definition of “cattle fair”; that defect was remedied by the amending legislation.

predicates.later_challenge_to_amended_statute: A party challenged the enforcement of a statute after it had been amended.
predicates.earlier_judgment_resting_on_uncured_defe: An earlier judgment had invalidated the original enactment on the basis of a defect in its then-existing text.
predicates.legislature_amended_statute_to_address_d: The legislature later changed the statute to address the defect identified in the earlier judgment.

issues.definition: When a later challenge concerns an amended statute and the legislature has addressed the defect on which an earlier judgment rested, that judgment does not bar enforcement of the amended statute.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction confined to arranging a large gathering for the specified purpose of a State-monopolised fair is a reasonable restriction on assembly and movement.
material_facts: The statute prohibited an individual or local authority from arranging a gathering of more than twenty-five persons for general sale or purchase of cattle.
It did not prohibit gatherings of twenty-five persons or fewer or generally restrict movement.
The restriction was imposed to make the State’s monopoly of conducting cattle fairs effective.
issues.conclusion: The restriction did not unreasonably infringe the freedoms of peaceful assembly or movement and was reasonable for the purposes of the constitutional limitations on those freedoms.
issues.legal_principle: The restriction was limited to arranging a gathering of more than twenty-five persons for the specified purpose and was necessary to make the State monopoly effective. It was therefore reasonable within the meaning of Articles 19(3) and 19(5), and did not infringe the rights under Article 19(1)(b) and (d).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_fair_restric: A party challenged a statutory restriction on arranging cattle-sale gatherings as an infringement of constitutional freedoms.
predicates.restriction_limited_to_large_cattle_sale: The restriction applied to arranging gatherings exceeding a specified size for general sale or purchase of cattle, rather than generally prohibiting assembly or movement.
predicates.restriction_serves_state_fair_monopoly: The restriction was imposed to make the State’s exclusive conduct of cattle fairs effective.

issues.definition: When a challenged restriction is confined to large cattle-sale gatherings and serves to make the State’s fair monopoly effective, it is reasonable and does not infringe assembly or movement.

issues.legal_issue: A prohibition on others conducting the same business is protected as an essential feature of a State monopoly and does not, on that account, infringe the freedoms to conduct business or to hold property.
material_facts: The legislation gave the State a monopoly to hold cattle fairs.
It prohibited individuals and local authorities from holding cattle fairs, a restriction directly necessary to make that monopoly effective.
The legislation did not extend the monopoly to every trade or occupation involving cattle.
issues.conclusion: The essential prohibition on others holding cattle fairs was not open to challenge as an unreasonable restriction on the freedoms to carry on business or to hold property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19(6), the basic and essential provisions necessary to create a State monopoly are protected against a challenge under Article 19(1)(g). Other provisions that are merely subsidiary or incidental must satisfy the ordinary test under Article 19(6). Akadasi Padhan v. State of Orissa, [1963] Supp. 2 SCR 691, was followed. The Court also held that the presumption of reasonableness of a State-monopoly statute may assist against a claim under Article 19(1)(f); State of Bihar v. Rameshwar Pratap Narain Singh, [1962] 2 SCR 382, and M. V. P. Ramunni Kurup v. Panchayat Board, Badagara, AIR 1954 Mad 754, were referred to but held not to determine the question.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_busine: A party challenged a law creating a State monopoly on the basis of constitutional freedoms relating to business or property.
predicates.prohibition_is_essential_to_create_monop: The challenged prohibition prevented others from conducting the same business and was basic and necessary to establish the State monopoly.

issues.definition: When a challenged prohibition is basic and necessary to create a State business monopoly, it is not invalidated under the freedoms relating to business or property on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory monopoly over cattle fairs does not extend to ordinary cattle markets or require a licence for market activity outside a lawfully declared fair area.
material_facts: The legislation reserved cattle fairs to the State and defined a cattle fair by reference to a gathering for general sale or purchase of cattle.
The activity challenged as a fair included a place where sheep and goats were regularly brought for sale, including for slaughter, rather than a gathering in the nature of a fair.
The statute did not prohibit conducting a cattle market on one’s own land, and the licensing requirement applied to business conducted within a lawfully declared fair area.
issues.conclusion: The legislation prohibited private parties from holding cattle fairs, not from conducting cattle markets; market activity outside a lawfully declared fair area did not require a broker’s licence under the Act.
issues.legal_principle: The State monopoly is confined to fairs and does not extend to cattle markets, meaning places where sale or purchase is regularly conducted by private parties rather than as a fair. A person carrying on business in a cattle market on their own land need not obtain a licence under section 9 merely because they collect brokerage; the licensing requirement applies to business within a lawfully declared fair area.

predicates.activity_is_regular_private_cattle_marke: Private parties regularly conducted sales or purchases of cattle at the place in question.
predicates.activity_not_conducted_as_fair: The activity was a market rather than a gathering conducted in the nature of a cattle fair.
predicates.business_outside_lawfully_declared_fair_: The business was not conducted within an area lawfully declared for a cattle fair.

issues.definition: When private parties regularly conduct a cattle market that is not a fair, outside a lawfully declared fair area, the activity is not prohibited as a fair or subject to fair-area licensing.

issues.legal_issue: The State’s monopoly to hold cattle fairs does not authorise it to use or requisition property belonging to local authorities or private owners without lawful authority and the required compensation.
material_facts: The legislation authorised the State to declare fair areas and to arrange and manage fairs, but did not expressly authorise the State to hold fairs on property belonging to local authorities or private owners.
The State sought to include municipal property in a fair area and to take possession of it for a fair.
The municipal property would be taken for the duration of the fair without the compensation required for such a taking.
A municipal committee is not a citizen entitled to claim Article 19 rights, but the constitutional protection against taking property without the required compensation remained applicable.
issues.conclusion: The State’s authority to hold and manage fairs was confined to State property; declaring local-authority or private property a fair area and taking possession of it without lawful authority and required compensation was unauthorised.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4 were interpreted consistently with constitutional protections: the State monopoly extends to holding fairs on State property, not property of local authorities or private owners. A municipal committee is not a “citizen” for Article 19, but taking its property without the compensation required by Article 31(2) is unauthorised. The statute’s paramount-operation provision cannot override a constitutional guarantee.

predicates.state_fair_monopoly: The law gives the State exclusive authority to hold and manage the relevant kind of fair.
predicates.proposed_fair_use_of_nonstate_property: The State sought to use property belonging to a local authority or private owner for the fair.
predicates.no_lawful_authority_for_taking_and_requi: The law did not authorise the taking of that property and the required compensation was not provided.

issues.definition: When the State’s fair monopoly is to be exercised on non-State property without lawful authority and required compensation, the State cannot use or requisition that property for the fair.

issues.legal_issue: A law cannot require a local authority to contribute money to a fund for the initial expenses of a State-run fair where the required contribution is an unreasonable deprivation of property.
material_facts: The statute authorised the State to direct a local authority within whose jurisdiction a fair would be held to deposit money in a fair fund for the fair’s initial expenses.
The local authority was required to comply with the direction.
Although the amount recovered could later be reimbursed from the fund, the Court found the compulsory payment unreasonable, and the State did not seek to support the provision.
issues.conclusion: The provision authorising the compulsory contribution was invalid as an unreasonable deprivation of property.
issues.legal_principle: The compulsory payment under section 15 deprived the local authority of property and was unreasonable, contrary to Article 19(1)(f). The possibility of reimbursement under section 17(d) did not save the provision.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_mandatory_lo: A party challenged a law requiring a local authority to fund the initial expenses of a fair conducted by the State.
predicates.local_authority_compelled_to_contribute: The law required the local authority to pay into a fund when directed, rather than making payment voluntary.
predicates.contribution_is_unreasonable_deprivation: The compulsory payment was found to be an unreasonable deprivation of the local authority’s property, notwithstanding possible later reimbursement.

issues.definition: When a local authority is compelled to contribute to State-run fair expenses and that payment is an unreasonable deprivation of property, the compulsory funding requirement is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory scheme for State-run fairs does not authorise officials to require a municipality to provide its property, staff, equipment, utilities or services for a fair.
material_facts: A fair officer and a district official required a municipality to make municipal land, staff, articles and offices available for a fair and to supply water and electricity and make sanitary arrangements.
The statute authorised the State to manage and regulate fairs but contained no provision authorising those demands.
The directions would have enabled the State to conduct the fair on municipal property.
issues.conclusion: The demands for municipal property, staff, articles, offices, water, electricity and sanitary arrangements were unauthorised and invalid.
issues.legal_principle: The powers conferred by sections 3 and 4 did not authorise officials to requisition municipal property or require municipal assistance and amenities. The State’s power to make arrangements for a fair was confined to State property, and the demands had no basis in the Act.

predicates.officials_demand_municipal_resources_for: Officials required a municipality to provide property, personnel, equipment, utilities or services for a State-run fair.
predicates.statute_does_not_authorise_municipal_ass: The governing law contained no authority for officials to compel the municipality to provide those resources.

issues.definition: When officials demand municipal resources for a State-run fair without statutory authority, those demands are invalid.
